title: Whose Knowledge Shapes the Decision?
before: Explore how accounts are received and recorded, and how relevant knowledge can reach a decision with its meaning intact.

turns.text: Whose Knowledge Shapes the Decision? is a course about how accounts are received, recorded, and allowed to influence what happens next. It’s for staff examining evidence and participation in service or workforce decisions, and for supervisors and managers thinking about whose contribution receives meaningful consideration. The course looks closely at credibility, categories, and influence.

The opening case is simple and uncomfortable: a service user describes a confusing handoff, and the concern is dismissed as a misunderstanding. Then a professional repeats the same concern, and it receives attention. The course asks what changed: the evidence, the explanation, or the speaker’s standing. It’s careful to say the comparison invites inquiry rather than establishing a motive.

The key idea comes from Fricker, who describes unfair credibility discounts and unequal access to the shared understanding we use to explain experience. In plain terms, someone’s account may receive less consideration than it deserves, or the categories we have may fail to describe it. Both possibilities need evidence in the particular situation.

That second possibility shows up in the course’s reporting form example. The form offers “technical problem” or “staff conduct,” but the person describes an unusable page followed by a dismissive response. Forcing one category can erase part of the account. The course asks how to keep valid definitions while making room for a sequence they don’t capture.

It also says something I think is important about silence. A person may be listening, preparing, tired, uncertain, or judging the setting unsuitable, and silence alone doesn’t tell you which. So instead of reading meaning into it, you invite contribution through routes people can use, without requiring personal disclosure or a public performance of commitment.

You’ll practice with that handoff concern that only gets reviewed after a professional repeats it. There’s a workplace example where an employee’s proposal gets attention and credit only after a senior colleague repeats it. And there’s a community participant whose account doesn’t fit either category on a practice form. Each one asks what a fair route would look like.

The workplace case shows why this matters beyond one meeting, because credit can shape access to development and later evidence of readiness. So the course asks you to look at the original contribution, its later reception, and the record of recognition together. It also notes that public recognition isn’t automatically the repair a person wants.

And influence depends on timing, because if the choice has already closed, a chance to comment may support understanding, but it can’t shape that decision. A correction should reach the next decision, too. An apology can matter without repairing the record, and no one has to forgive or join a learning discussion to receive a proper response.

Near the end, you’ll rewrite a story that takes over someone’s meaning: “Our quiet employees needed a senior voice to explain their needs.” The supported version simply describes what the employee identified and when it received review. You’ll then consider what correction would preserve the original contribution and address the route itself.

The reflection asks you to recall a time when a title, confident delivery, or familiar language made an account easier for you to accept, and what evidence you actually examined. It stays private, and the point isn’t to dismiss either expertise or lived experience, but to ask fairer questions of both.

As you begin, think of a decision in your work that drew on several people’s input, perhaps a service review, a team proposal, or a complaint record. Whose account shaped the outcome, and whose took longer to be heard? Keep that example in mind, and notice what a fair route from knowledge to decision would require.

guidance.title: Two ways knowledge can be lost
guidance.text: The course names two different problems. In one, a person’s account is heard but given less weight than the evidence warrants. In the other, the available categories or language can’t hold what happened, so the account loses its shape before anyone weighs it. Each calls for a different repair, which is why the particular situation needs careful examination.

guidance.title: Hearing the substance first
guidance.text: Think about how accounts reach decisions in your work, through notes, forms, meetings, or summaries. Where might a concern lose its meaning or its attribution along the way? What question could you ask to receive the substance before considering who said it, and how would you make sure a correction reaches the next decision?
